detail.findings_tradeoffs: Supply-chain attacks caused by developer compromise are a common story, but imagine what happens if ongoing mitigation attempts, including work by Trail of Bits 2 , are successful. If developers of popular packages are no longer the easiest targets, attackers will shift their focus to the next weakest link in the system: the package repositories that serve the code. The cryptographic answers to this problem are more subtle than they appear, and many implementations fall short due to deliberate design choices, resource prioritization, or the complexity of developer-friendly solutions. One natural answer is to include a cryptographic hash of a package’s contents in a lockfile and compare hashes after downloading the package. This automatic verification was the default behavior in about half of the package managers I tested, but others required extra configuration to include or verify these hashes, used hashes in a cryptographically insecure way, or lacked hashes entirely. This is summarized in the following table. Verifies integrity Go, vcpkg Verifies if lockfile is present Bun, Bundler, Cargo, npm, pnpm, Poetry, SwiftPM, uv, Yarn Verifies with lockfile + extra steps Conda, Gradle, Pip, NuGet, Pub Does not verify with lockfile or N/A CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, cpanminus, Gem, Maven, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, R Table 1: Lockfile-based security of a package manager fetching dependencies from a malicious repository, categorized by how much work it takes a developer to achieve integrity. Experimentally verified for a particular configuration. Caveats detailed below. Another natural approach is to use signatures, avoiding the need to securely distribute a hash for every package. However, in my tests, only Go verified signatures by default; others required extra configuration, lacked verification code, or did not support signatures. Verifies signatures Go Verifies with configuration Bundler, Gem, Gradle, Maven, npm, NuGet Missing or incomplete verification Bun, cpanminus, Pip, pnpm, Poetry, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, uv, Yarn No signatures available for verification Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, SwiftPM, vcpkg Table 2: Signature-based security of various package managers. Also experimentally verified and subject to similar caveats. As both tables show, I found a surprising variation in the cryptographic designs and the level of protection they provide. Despite the challenges, I also found several communities on the frontier of this integrity problem that are bringing improved designs to reality. This post explores those variations, showing where certain designs fall short, why code integrity is harder to solve than it appears, and what cryptographic designs might be adopted in the future. Simulating malicious package repositories Studying the cryptographic behavior of 25 package managers is quite the challenge. I wanted to minimize manual analysis, but also be 100% confident when I claim an attack from a malicious package repository is possible. To solve this problem, I built a testing harness based on Docker containers and mitmproxy that dynamically evaluates the security of package managers against a malicious server. Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon. Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful. I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is. With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear. HTTPS is (almost) everywhere Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are. The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior. 3 Hash functions don’t always provide integrity By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place. Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository. 4 Hashes in lockfiles It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s. This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift). Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock . NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project. Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile 5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock ) without hashes in them. Hashes present, but not for integrity Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another. The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package. uuid : dependency : "direct main" description : name : uuid sha256 : "9b129329f58692f6e6578329498a8fe9fbe98f090beb764ffbb8ee2eadd01dcd" url : "https://pub.dev" source : hosted version : "4.6.0" If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway. The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for: * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev" This indicates one of: * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock. * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted. The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated. This is documented behavior , and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation 6 . Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected. Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++. "requires" : [ "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337" ] , This includes the package name ( zlib ), the version number ( 1.3.1 ), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20 , and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash. The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency. SPEC CHECKSUMS : Files : d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec , which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository. "source" : { "git" : "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git" , "tag" : "4.0.2" } , So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag. Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt. "dist" : { "type" : "zip" , "url" : "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "reference" : "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "shasum" : "" } , However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer. Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example. Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm , pnpm , Poetry , uv , and Yarn ), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler ), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo ). Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches. The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation. Signatures are common; verification is not Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem. Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM 7 . The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity. Repository signing One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure. Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry , the NuGet Registry , and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys . NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys . The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time. Developer signing Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader. There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers . RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec ). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed . The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA , and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys. One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key. Identity-based signing An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore . Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature. Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing 8 . GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code. Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI , the npm Registry , RubyGems repository , and Maven Central . While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys. Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers. In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install . Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures , which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command , but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command. In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept , which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source . These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers. Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys ( gem cert --add ) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification , which works similarly. Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. Acknowledgments Thank you to William Woodruff for valuable discussions about lockfiles, identity signing, and the challenges of package manager security. This post focuses on dependency managers for source code rather than system package managers like APT, Chocolatey, or Homebrew. The line between the two is blurred, but concentrating on one helps highlight particular usage and deployment patterns in that group. ↩︎ Trail of Bits has several ongoing and completed projects to improve supply-chain security in some of these package ecosystems, including helping address both account takeover threats and the cryptographic integrity problem. ↩︎ cpanminus is included in the default Docker container for Perl , but the container build scripts patch cpanminus to use HTTPS by default. ↩︎ A subtle distinction here is that vcpkg must be updated using git pull in order to fetch the latest package hashes, shifting the question from securely installing packages to securely updating the package manager. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎ Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎ Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test , call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub . ↩︎ The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification. The latter supports signatures, and the server protocol is implemented by private services such as JFrog Artifactory and AWS CodeArtifact . As far as I can find, there is no repository for the general public that implements this protocol, so I tested the signatureless Git format. ↩︎ Trusted publishing can also refer to using OIDC tokens to authenticate to a package repository, and it does not necessarily involve identity-based signing. ↩︎ Although I did not test PowerShell on Windows, the documented default ExecutionPolicy behavior is to block scripts on Windows client machines, and to require a valid signature for Windows servers. This achieves package integrity. ↩︎ Go calls these downloadable artifacts “modules,” which consist of “packages.” For the sake of consistent terminology with the rest of the post, I use “package” in the general sense, not the Go-specific one. ↩︎ The go.sum file stores hashes, but it is not a lockfile . Instead, it is a local cache for entries from the checksum database. ↩︎

Figure 1: Experimental design of the test harness used to simulate malicious package repositories The Ubuntu-based Docker images include a package manager, sample code, and optionally a lockfile. There are conflicting opinions about whether to include lockfiles in source code repositories, so I tested both configurations. The harness instructs the package manager to fetch dependencies from the repository, and the resulting network request routes through a WireGuard network to a custom mitmproxy addon. Because the mitmproxy TLS CA is installed in the Docker image, the addon can fully manipulate the plaintext from the package repository, simulating a compromised server. I assumed any web-facing server could be compromised (e.g., Composer fetches metadata from Packagist and packages from GitHub), but backend resources, like any private signing keys, remain secure. The simulated repository embeds malicious code into the downloaded packages, and if the sample code executes the malware, the attack is successful. I tried to keep the experimental setup reflective of real-world usage, but there are limitations. I installed the latest package manager versions, followed quickstart guides for setting up sample projects inside the container, and picked popular packages from public repositories to infect. I ran package manager commands with default flags to see if extra steps, like modifying the project manifest or running extra commands, were needed to enforce cryptographic integrity. However, I am limited to testing a single package with a single package manager version on a single platform, and the test conditions (e.g., PowerShell and CocoaPods on Ubuntu) may not represent the most common usage patterns. The setup isn’t meant to show that every developer is vulnerable to a malicious package repository, just that a developer following reasonable conventions is. With the package managers installed and network intercept functional, one (mostly) promising observation is clear. HTTPS is (almost) everywhere Our harness architecture captures all network traffic, so it’s easy to test that package managers are using TLS and validating the certificates. In almost every package manager, they are. The exception is cpanminus, the frequently recommended package manager for Perl. cpanminus uses unencrypted HTTP by default to connect to the Perl package repository, allowing any active network attacker to inject malicious code into downloaded packages. This vulnerability has been known for years, but the cpanminus developer has not switched to HTTPS, since doing so would be a breaking change to default behavior. 3 Hash functions don’t always provide integrity By using the mitmproxy addon to modify the package repository responses, I could investigate how different package managers use cryptographic hashes. Hashes are a natural way to ensure that a downloaded file has not been tampered with, but the main question is how the package manager learns the correct hash in the first place. Microsoft’s vcpkg package manager for C and C++ libraries offers an interesting example. The package manager source code includes content hashes for thousands of dependencies. When a developer updates their library and wants to register the new content in vcpkg, they recompute the hash of their package and open a pull request against the vcpkg source code with the new hash and link to the package. When a package is downloaded by vcpkg, the hash is checked. So as long as the package manager is trusted, this approach is fully secure against a malicious package repository. 4 Hashes in lockfiles It is significantly more common that the package manager learns the correct hash via a lockfile. A lockfile is frequently created by a package manager, resides alongside a project’s source code, and references specific versions of dependencies needed by the project. If a developer checks a lockfile with cryptographic hashes into the source code repository, and the user’s package manager validates downloaded packages against the hashes, then the user’s dependencies perfectly match the developer’s. This is how it works for the Bun package manager for JavaScript projects. Installing a package with bun add updates the bun.lock lockfile; committing the lockfile to Git and calling bun install on another copy of the repo verifies the hash in the lockfile against the new copy of the dependency. Similar behavior is found in npm, pnpm, and Yarn (also JavaScript package managers); uv and Poetry (Python package managers); Bundler (for Ruby); Cargo (for Rust); and SwiftPM (for Swift). Other package managers support lockfiles, but with more steps than the standard add/restore process. Python’s Pip has experimental support for the pylock.toml format, and Conda has the optional library Conda lock . NuGet, the .NET package manager, generates a lockfile after adding the RestorePackagesWithLockFile property to the project. Many package managers (Maven, R, PowerShellGet, PSResourceGet, and cpanminus) do not have dedicated lockfiles, and some have lockfiles (Gradle’s gradle.lockfile 5 and Gem’s Gemfile.lock ) without hashes in them. Hashes present, but not for integrity Surprisingly, I found a few examples where the lockfiles had a hash, but could still be compromised by a malicious server. This is not necessarily reflective of a vulnerability, since the underlying behavior is clearly documented, but it shows how there are multiple valid opinions about how lockfiles should be structured and consumed. Nevertheless, a user who is accustomed to the behavior of one package manager may be surprised by that of another. The first example is the Pub package manager for Dart and Flutter. The following excerpt of a pubspec.lock file includes a SHA-256 hash for the uuid package. uuid : dependency : "direct main" description : name : uuid sha256 : "9b129329f58692f6e6578329498a8fe9fbe98f090beb764ffbb8ee2eadd01dcd" url : "https://pub.dev" source : hosted version : "4.6.0" If a user calls flutter pub get to fetch dependencies, Pub downloads the package from the pub.dev server and computes the hash of the returned binary. If there is a mismatch, Pub detects the error, but installs the package anyway. The existing content-hash from pubspec.lock doesn't match contents for: * uuid-4.6.0 from "https://pub.dev" This indicates one of: * The content has changed on the server since you created the pubspec.lock. * The pubspec.lock has been corrupted. The content-hashes in pubspec.lock has been updated. This is documented behavior , and requires the non-default --enforce-lockfile option to block installation 6 . Overwriting the lockfile after a hash mismatch was also the default behavior in pnpm until version 11.4 from May 2026, when it was changed to close “supply-chain holes.” Like Pub, pnpm also supported a non-default --frozen-lockfile flag, indicating that the previous behavior which updated the lockfile was expected. Next, here is an excerpt of a conan.lock file, used by the Conan package manager for C and C++. "requires" : [ "zlib/1.3.1#cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20%1765284699.337" ] , This includes the package name ( zlib ), the version number ( 1.3.1 ), a recipe revision cac0f6daea041b0ccf42934163defb20 , and a timestamp. The 128-bit revision is an MD5 hash that includes source code. However, this hash is not intended to provide cryptographic security, but rather serves as a unique identifier. When Conan installs dependencies using this lockfile, it uses the recipe revision hash to download a particular file from the ConanCenter repository, but it does not recompute the recipe hash. Even if it did, there’s a separate package revision hash for platform-specific binaries that is not in the lockfile, and MD5 collisions could allow an attacker to create two distinct recipes with different behavior but the same hash. The CocoaPods dependency manager for Swift and Objective-C has a similar pattern. Here is part of a Podfile.lock file for a project that uses the popular Files dependency. SPEC CHECKSUMS : Files : d88e31b84d65e754935053b1c584ea8e2320698a This 160-bit checksum is the SHA-1 hash of the Files Podspec , which contains the following link to the source code. CocoaPods uses this link to fetch the Git repository. "source" : { "git" : "https://github.com/johnsundell/files.git" , "tag" : "4.0.2" } , So even though the lockfile can prevent tampering with the GitHub URL in the Podspec (setting aside expensive SHA-1 collision attacks), a compromised GitHub server could just serve a malicious version of the repository with the same tag. Finally, the Composer dependency manager for PHP includes commit hashes in the composer.lock file, as in the following excerpt. "dist" : { "type" : "zip" , "url" : "https://api.github.com/repos/guzzle/psr7/zipball/b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "reference" : "b094ded77ee97a6027ad6cf0e8c7b9f88381814c" , "shasum" : "" } , However, even though the b094ded... commit hash uniquely identifies the code, the ZIP archive in the URL does not include the Git tree as a way to verify the hash. Once again, GitHub could serve a malicious ZIP archive without detection by Composer. Lockfiles have many roles besides supply-chain integrity The previous experimental results show that lockfile hashes often can be used to enforce package integrity, but this is not their sole or even original purpose. Alternatively, they can lock dependencies to a particular functionality, enable an easy way for application developers to share a consistent environment, or facilitate reproducible builds. Analyzing package manager lockfiles through the lens of supply-chain security is a recent interpretation that can be at odds with their original design. The recent change to pnpm’s --frozen-lockfile is one example. Another example of this tension is the question of whether the lockfile should be committed to version control. Most modern guidance recommends committing the lockfile for applications, since the final build environment is fully controlled. The question is more complicated for libraries, since package managers often ignore libraries’ lockfiles to avoid locking to conflicting transitive dependencies. Committing the lockfile makes it easier to develop the library by sharing a consistent build environment with other developers, but excluding the lockfile makes it easier to catch conflicts with different dependency versions before they are found by users. Many package managers recommend committing the lockfile for libraries (e.g., npm , pnpm , Poetry , uv , and Yarn ), some recommend excluding it (e.g., Bundler ), and some leave it up to the developer (e.g., Cargo ). Many of these questions are explored in a recent study by Gamage et al. The authors explore lockfile design decisions for seven package managers, analyze published projects, and perform semi-structured interviews with 15 developers. They find that the practice of committing a lockfile varies by which package manager is used, and categorize five benefits to using lockfiles, as perceived by the interview subjects: build determinism, integrity, transparency into indirect dependencies, debugging, and security scanning. Some of the developers also preferred to not use lockfiles, citing a preference for end users to resolve to the latest version of a dependency, which may have more bug fixes and vulnerability patches. The diversity of package manager designs and views surrounding the purpose of lockfiles makes it difficult to prescribe a single recommendation. With regard to supply-chain integrity, it is common, but not universal, to view lockfiles as a source of integrity that should be committed with the source code. For package managers with lockfiles that do not provide cryptographic integrity, it is worth considering whether their users share that expectation. Even when lockfile hashes can provide cryptographic integrity, locking to specific package hashes means that users do not immediately receive subsequent updates or security fixes, since the newer package has a different hash. This leads to frequent lockfile bumping to distribute the latest hashes. Wanting immediate updates is a separate concern from wanting package integrity, but the current, common approach of using hashes in lockfiles is at odds with that goal. In conclusion, lockfile hashes are often, but not always, effective at providing cryptographic integrity, but do not work in every situation. Signatures are common; verification is not Signatures are a natural way to address these shortcomings, but implementations frequently fall short. In theory, developers could sign every release with their own private key, and the package manager could check the signature of the package it downloads from the package repository. In fact, signatures are relatively common in different package ecosystems, but proper signature validation is surprisingly lacking. The reality of using signatures to provide code integrity is more nuanced than it seems, and package managers have different approaches to the problem. Many package managers have no signatures available. Arguably, vcpkg does not need them, because all package hashes are distributed with the manager, but this leaves Cargo, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, Pub, R, and SwiftPM 7 . The Conan developers are aware and previously decided not to fix it, citing several implementation challenges and suggesting organizations where integrity is critical could run their own repository server. Cargo developers are actively considering different signing designs, but this effort is still in progress. Composer developers have been implementing many new protections against supply-chain attacks, with future plans for artifact integrity. Repository signing One straightforward approach, known as repository signing, is when the package repository signs every package once it’s uploaded, and the repository’s public key is distributed with the package manager. This doesn’t solve the problem of a totally compromised package repository, since a malicious package repository could legitimately sign a malicious package, but it would protect against untrusted mirrors or a partial compromise of a package repository’s serving infrastructure. Repository signatures are used by the npm Registry , the NuGet Registry , and the PAUSE server for Perl module distribution. In the npm Registry, signatures are distributed within package metadata with repository-specific public keys . NuGet Registry repository signatures are found in .signature.p7s files within the distributed ZIP package, again with repository-specific public keys . The PAUSE server takes a different approach, using its GPG key to batch sign the cryptographic hashes of several packages at a time. Developer signing Developer signing involves the developer maintaining the private key and signing the package before uploading it to the repository for distribution. This prevents the package repository from tampering with the contents, but it also provides a way for the package repository to authenticate the uploader. There are two common approaches for a developer asserting their public key. In the first approach, the public key is distributed out-of-band. The Maven Central repository (used by Maven and Gradle) and the RubyGems repository (used by the gem and Bundler package managers) both support this type of developer signing. Maven Central uses PGP signatures, and developer keys are distributed by public keyservers . RubyGems uses self-signed certificates, and their distribution is left to the developers (e.g., rspec ). The major difference is that developer signing is mandatory for Maven Central, and optional for RubyGems. Developer signing is rare for RubyGems, due to the lack of an established chain of trust, and a previous attempt to introduce a certificate authority failed . The second approach involves a chain of trust. The NuGet Registry and PowerShell Gallery both support developer signatures. Neither makes signatures mandatory, but the PowerShell Gallery recommends it and the NuGet Registry has strict requirements if developer signing is used. In both, the developer’s key must chain to a trusted CA , and acquiring a valid code-signing certificate can cost hundreds of dollars per year. The benefit of this approach is that trusted root certificates can be preinstalled on the platform, allowing package managers to verify public keys. One downside of developer signing is that developers are responsible for key management, and they can lose the ability to update their code if they lose access to their key. Identity-based signing An increasingly common middle ground is “identity-based” or “keyless” signing from Sigstore . Rather than require developers to manage long-term private keys, a developer can use Sigstore’s Fulcio CA to issue a fresh signing certificate on demand, for free. To prevent impersonation, the developer proves their identity with an OIDC token: a cryptographically signed statement from a third party like Google, Microsoft, or GitHub that attests to the email address, username, or potentially other claims about the developer’s identity. The verifier can check that the username is correct and the certificate chain links back to Sigstore Fulcio’s root certificate, proving that someone with access to that account created the signature. Keyless signing is particularly useful because it can be integrated into a developer’s existing workflow-based deployment pipeline. This is frequently called provenance attestation or trusted publishing 8 . GitHub and GitLab provide OIDC tokens to Actions and CI/CD workflows that attest to the build workflow, the repository, and the commit hash. A workflow can use this token to obtain a signing certificate from Sigstore, sign the built package, and upload the signed package to the package repository. Since the signing certificate includes the commit hash and workflow details, this cryptographically links the built binary artifact to its source code. Provenance attestation via Sigstore is supported by Python’s PyPI , the npm Registry , RubyGems repository , and Maven Central . While Sigstore attestations are not mandatory, there is already better adoption than RubyGems’ optional support for developer-managed signing keys. Verification code is skipped, unconfigured, or nonexistent Unfortunately, just because these signatures exist does not mean they are being verified by package managers. In the npm package manager, the repository signatures are not checked when running npm install . Checking the signatures requires running npm audit signatures , which uses Sigstore to validate the registry public keys and then validates the signatures of the installed packages. pnpm recently added the pnpm audit signatures command , but that implementation fetches the registry public keys from the potentially malicious registry rather than verifying with Sigstore, so an adversary could simply add their own key and signature. Bun and Yarn currently lack an equivalent audit signatures command. In the NuGet package manager, the default signatureValidationMode is accept , which installs invalidly signed packages. The user must set this to require and configure the list of trusted signers, such as with dotnet nuget trust source . These configurations (which include the repository public keys) can be securely distributed within a nuget.config configuration file, functioning as a lockfile that locks the trusted signers. Ruby’s Gem and Bundler, and Java’s Maven and Gradle, which all use repositories with developer signatures, do not verify signatures by default. They require the user to manually add developer public keys ( gem cert --add ) or list the allowed public keys that should be trusted. In Maven, one can use the third-party pgpverify-maven-plugin with pgp-keys-map.list to specify the trusted PGP fingerprints. Gradle offers dependency verification , which works similarly. Finally, several package managers seemingly lack any sort of verification code at all. Pip , uv , and Poetry do not currently have a way to verify identity-based attestations described in PEP740. cpanminus does not have a way to verify the integrity of the repository-signed CHECKSUMS file. It once did, but in response to a verification bypass vulnerability , this verification code was removed . Even though PowerShell is supported on non-Windows platforms, Authenticode signature verification is not 9 . At one point, the PowerShell repository noted that this issue “should be fixed in a future release.” Go package management and transparency logs Go’s built-in package manager is the only one I tested that verifies signatures by default, and it also introduces one final concept for cryptographic package integrity. When go get or go mod download fetches a package 10 , it hashes the package contents and compares the hash, package name, and version against the checksum database . The contents of the database are registry-signed (analogous to PGP signatures in Perl’s PAUSE server), and the default checksum database public key is hardcoded in Go’s source code. As long as the checksum database’s private key is used honestly, this design ensures that the package name and version are enough to uniquely identify the binary contents of a package. As a result, the go.mod lockfile achieves package integrity without needing to store cryptographic hashes. 11 Go’s checksum database is an example of a transparency log, or an immutable, global, tamper-resistant log of metadata. The same capability is provided by Sigstore’s Rekor and certificate transparency logs. In package managers, it cryptographically ensures that the package manager only ever installs the same binaries recorded by the transparency log. If everyone agrees on the transparency log, then everyone agrees on the package contents. This makes it more difficult for an adversary to selectively and undetectably target a victim with a malicious package. Transparency logs can still fail if there are other vulnerabilities , the log’s private key is compromised, or no one checks the transparency log for malicious behavior. Of all the package managers I tested, Go performed the best at maintaining cryptographic integrity in the face of a compromised package repository or proxy. However, the registry-signature-like design means that much of the system’s trust is concentrated in a single private key. A proposed cryptographic design for package managers One potential approach that combines the ideas in this post is to include signature information in the lockfile. Rather than commit to the hash of a particular package, the lockfile could commit to a developer’s identity or public key. This reuses much of the infrastructure in place for lockfile hashes, but it separates the question of immediate updates from the question of package integrity. With this design, the lockfile could specify a single dependency version (for build reproducibility) or a lower bound (for immediate updates), and the included identity ensures that a malicious repository or proxy cannot easily tamper with whatever package version the manager resolves to. In addition, a transparency log can protect against selective targeting, building on Sigstore’s identity-based signing and transparency log service. Sigstore avoids long-lived keys by default, but it also supports self-managed keys, KMS providers, and hardware tokens. This gives an easily adopted and secure default while still giving flexibility to developers who desire more control over their keys. This idea is not new and not my own. Attestation identities are part of the pylock.toml Python lockfile specification , the trusted-keys in Gradle’s verification metadata , and the pgp-keys-map.list file in the pgpverify-maven-plugin for Maven. This is the direction that many package managers are already moving towards, as evidenced by the increasing adoption of Sigstore into publishing workflows, attention on supply-chain security, and bugfixes that specifically cite potential tampering by a malicious adversary. There is increasing recognition that this is a problem, and increasing appetite to fix it. It won’t be easy. There are many subtle nuances that have to be considered and addressed, signing verification code needs to be developed and audited, and developers need to adopt the resulting design. In many of the package managers I reviewed as part of this project, I found communities of people who have been thinking about and pushing for cryptographic integrity and package signing for years. They know best what those package managers need, and they deserve the resources to make this a reality. One of the greatest cryptographic success stories in the past decade has been the nearly universal adoption of HTTPS, driven in part by industry and community recognition of the security risks of unencrypted traffic, and the nonprofit Let’s Encrypt providing free and easy-to-use TLS certificates as a public good. Package signing is in a similar state now to where HTTPS was a decade ago: persistent adversaries are a huge concern, and cryptographic security is nearly nonexistent. Universal package signing is not here yet, but it is on the horizon. With the right attention and investment, we can make it a reality. Acknowledgments Thank you to William Woodruff for valuable discussions about lockfiles, identity signing, and the challenges of package manager security. This post focuses on dependency managers for source code rather than system package managers like APT, Chocolatey, or Homebrew. The line between the two is blurred, but concentrating on one helps highlight particular usage and deployment patterns in that group. ↩︎ Trail of Bits has several ongoing and completed projects to improve supply-chain security in some of these package ecosystems, including helping address both account takeover threats and the cryptographic integrity problem. ↩︎ cpanminus is included in the default Docker container for Perl , but the container build scripts patch cpanminus to use HTTPS by default. ↩︎ A subtle distinction here is that vcpkg must be updated using git pull in order to fetch the latest package hashes, shifting the question from securely installing packages to securely updating the package manager. For consistency with other package managers, we do not consider this question, and we note this as a limitation of our threat model. ↩︎ Gradle can have a verification-metadata.xml file with content hashes, even though gradle.lockfile does not. ↩︎ Note that some flutter subcommands, including flutter run and flutter test , call flutter pub get by default, so these commands can also overwrite the pubspec.lock file unless called with --no-pub . ↩︎ The SwiftPM client has two main ways to download packages: via Git and via the custom Swift Package Registry Service Specification. The latter supports signatures, and the server protocol is implemented by private services such as JFrog Artifactory and AWS CodeArtifact . As far as I can find, there is no repository for the general public that implements this protocol, so I tested the signatureless Git format. ↩︎ Trusted publishing can also refer to using OIDC tokens to authenticate to a package repository, and it does not necessarily involve identity-based signing. ↩︎ Although I did not test PowerShell on Windows, the documented default ExecutionPolicy behavior is to block scripts on Windows client machines, and to require a valid signature for Windows servers. This achieves package integrity. ↩︎ Go calls these downloadable artifacts “modules,” which consist of “packages.” For the sake of consistent terminology with the rest of the post, I use “package” in the general sense, not the Go-specific one. ↩︎ The go.sum file stores hashes, but it is not a lockfile . Instead, it is a local cache for entries from the checksum database. ↩︎

items.headline: Rethinking Zero-Knowledge TLS: Proof of Protocol Execution and the Reclaim Protocol
items.summary: In a zkTLS protocol, a user proves to a third party a property of data obtained from an online service over TLS, revealing nothing beyond the statement proven. Each existing scheme, however, comes with its own security model, written for that scheme alone, so the schemes are not proven secure against a common definition. The root cause is a mismatch of levels: existing models are stated at the level of TLS and therefore reflect how each construction handles it.

detail.problem_context: In a zkTLS protocol, a user proves to a third party a property of data obtained from an online service over TLS, revealing nothing beyond the statement proven.
detail.method_architecture: Each existing scheme, however, comes with its own security model, written for that scheme alone, so the schemes are not proven secure against a common definition. The root cause is a mismatch of levels: existing models are stated at the level of TLS and therefore reflect how each construction handles it.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: Yet TLS is only the transport, and a zkTLS proof is about the application-layer protocol executed over it. We therefore introduce the first transport-agnostic security model for zkTLS, stated at the application layer and mentioning neither TLS nor any particular construction. The resulting notion, Zero-Knowledge Proof of Protocol Execution (zkPoPE), defines what it means for a party that has executed an arbitrary two-party protocol with a counterparty to prove, in zero knowledge, that its private input and the reply it received satisfy a chosen property, and, crucially, that the reply comes from a real execution with that counterparty rather than being fabricated. This proof-of-execution requirement separates zkPoPE from a NIZK over the input--reply pair: knowing a satisfying pair does not by itself show that an execution occurred. We formalize zkPoPE as a UC ideal functionality F_{zkpope}. We then introduce the Reclaim Protocol, a zkTLS scheme that UC-realizes F_{zkpope} under a deployment-aligned trust model and underlies a production system. Reclaim builds on Distributed-AEAD, a new three-party authenticated-encryption primitive of independent interest. On a lower-mid-range phone, Reclaim attests to a 1200kB response in 7.28s, two orders of magnitude beyond any size previously benchmarked for zkTLS.

items.headline: On the Security of MPC-in-the-Head Signatures with Correlated GGM Trees
items.summary: Recent MPC-in-the-Head techniques enable the construction of signature schemes with compact signature sizes from various hardness assumptions. These techniques rely on commitments based on GGM trees, which have been optimized to further reduce the signature size with the so-called one-tree or correlated tree optimizations. While the one-tree technique has no incidence on the security of the scheme, this is not obvious for the correlated tree technique, and a formal security analysis of this technique has been missing in the literature.

items.headline: Phoenix: Hash-and-Sign with Aborts from Lattice Gadgets
items.summary: Preimage sampling is a fundamental tool in lattice-based cryptography, and its performance directly impacts that of the cryptographic mechanisms relying on it. In 2012, Micciancio and Peikert proposed a new way of generating trapdoors (and an associated preimage sampling procedure) with very interesting features. Unfortunately, in some applications such as digital signatures, the performance may not be as competitive as other approaches like Fiat-Shamir with Aborts.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: In an effort to improve preimage sampling for Micciancio-Peikert (MP) trapdoors, Lyubashevsky and Wichs (LW) introduced a new sampler which leverages rejection sampling but suffers from strong parameter requirements that hampered performance. As a consequence it seemed to be restricted to theoretical applications and has not been, to our knowledge, considered for real-world applications. Our first contribution is to revisit the LW sampler by proposing an improved analysis which yields much more compact parameters. This leads to gains on the preimage size of about 60% over the LW sampler, and up to 25% compared to the original MP sampling technique. It thus sheds a new light on the LW sampler, opening promising perspectives for the efficiency of advanced lattice-based constructions relying on such mechanisms. To provide further improvements, we show that it perfectly combines with the approximate trapdoors approach by Chen, Genise and Mukherjee, but with a smaller preimage error. Building upon those results, we introduce a hash-and-sign signature scheme called Phoenix. The scheme is based on the M-LWE and M-SIS assumptions and features attractive public key and signature sizes which are even smaller than those of the most recent gadget-based construction Eagle of Yu, Jia and Wang (Crypto’23). Moreover, Phoenix is designed to be implementation-friendly, avoiding in particular complex Gaussian samplers that are often hard to protect.

items.headline: Ideal Pseudorandom Code, Revisited
items.summary: Pseudorandom error-correcting codes (PRCs), introduced by Christ and Gunn at CRYPTO’24, combine pseudorandomness with error correction, providing a natural abstraction for robust watermarking and steganography on generative AI models. Subsequent standalone notions, which are ideal security for secret-key PRCs and CCA-style security for public-key PRCs, are oracle-based and do not capture composable use with explicit parties, sessions, and corruption. We give a UC treatment of PRCs via corruption-aware ideal functionalities for both settings.

items.headline: Aker: Efficient Two-Party SLH-DSA
items.summary: Threshold signing is widely deployed to protect cryptographic keys, but extending these deployments to post-quantum signatures remains challenging. While NIST's lattice-based signatures now have efficient threshold protocols, distributed signing for SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), NIST's stateless hash-based signature standard, has been considered prohibitively expensive because it lacks the algebraic structure those protocols typically exploit. We present Aker, a maliciously secure two-party signing protocol compatible with an unmodified FIPS 205 verifier.

items.headline: Sunshine Systems: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Compliance with Freedom of Information Laws
items.summary: Freedom of information laws (informally known as Sunshine Laws), such as the US Federal Freedom of Information Act, provide legal pathways for members of the public to compel governments to produce internal documentation. These laws have become a powerful tool for government accountability, allowing journalists and activists to uncover malfeasance and advocate for change. However, because compliance with these laws requires government actors---the same entities who may be accused of malfeasance---to produce documentation, there is a risk that evidence of malfeasance may be suppressed rather than produced in response to a query.

items.headline: QUASI: Post-Quantum Quorum Attestation of Pre-Validated Statements
items.summary: We present QUASI, a newly conceived class of hash-based, post-quantum-secure protocols that enable a group of parties to produce a publicly verifiable attestation about a pre-validated statement. QUASI produces attestations that reduce the size and verification cost to a fraction of a full hash-based signatures collection, without relying on SNARKs or a trusted setup. QUASI rests on a surprising discovery: each party need not sign the entire statement.

items.headline: How Will the 340B Rebate Model Pilot Affect Covered Entity Finances? -- by Charles J. Courtemanche
items.summary: The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) plans to implement a pilot switching 340B from an upfront discount model to a rebate model for drugs in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program (MDPNP). This study uses calibration methods to predict the impact of the rebate model pilot (RMP) on covered entities’ net revenues from the 340B program. I examine possible losses from averted duplicate discounts; denial of valid claims; manufacturers using data to exert influence; liquidity-related expenses; and administrative and staffing costs.

items.headline: Horizontal Equity of Taxation: Citizen Beliefs and Policy Preferences -- by Pierre Bachas, Christopher A. Hoy, Anders Jensen, Mahvish Shaukat
items.summary: Taxes are harder to enforce on the self-employed than on wage earners, creating horizontal inequities among taxpayers with similar incomes. Using tax microsimulation and household survey data from 29 developing countries, we show that horizontal inequities in actual tax systems are comparable in magnitude to vertical equity and are exacerbated by progressive reforms that fall disproportionately on wage earners. We then conduct surveys and randomized information experiments in Pakistan to study public perceptions of these inequities.

items.headline: Monetary policy in a Phelps–Winter Economy -- by Bruce C. Greenwald, Joseph E. Stiglitz
items.summary: We use the Phelps-Winter customer market—providing a better theory of price determination for large parts of the economy than the standard model—to show that raising interest rates induces higher prices, as firms value current profits more, and are more willing to lose customers for short-term gains. These inflationary effects can be significant in relevant ranges of interest rates; they exist in the short run even when interest rate hikes succeed in cutting aggregate demand; and that they are amplified by policy uncertainty and the uncertainty about the effects of interest rate changes, both of which have increased as conventional policy has demonstrably failed badly to keep inflation at the 2% target. Empirical studies confirm this low level of ineffectiveness of raising interest rates in reducing inflation.

items.headline: Measuring the Impact of Impact Measurement -- by Emanuele Colonnelli, Timothy McQuade, Natalia Rigol, Benjamin N. Roth
items.summary: Impact measurement is central to impact investing and social entrepreneurship, yet little is known about whether firms benefit privately from measuring impact. items.headline: Gambling for Goals -- by Costas Arkolakis, Spencer Y. Kwon, Dominic Russel, Claire Shi, Hyunjoo Yang
items.summary: Young adults in advanced economies have grown more pessimistic about their economic prospects in recent years. At the same time, gambling-like financial activities have proliferated. We link these trends through a Friedman-Savage (1948) motive: when life goals such as homeownership or marriage seem out of reach, individuals turn to financial gambles.

items.headline: Investment and Governance: Through The Lens of Sustainability -- by Jitendra Aswani, Roberto Rigobon
items.summary: Using 3,944 sustainable bond issuances by public firms from 2013 to 2022, we examine the causal effect of sustainable investment on governance adoption. A heteroskedasticity-based identification strategy reveals that a 1% increase in sustainable debt (by total debt) raises the likelihood of sustainable governance adoption by 9.2%. Such adoption improves environmental performance by 16% (structural estimates).

items.headline: Last-Mile Delivery and the Future of Aid -- by Erika Deserranno, Andrea Guariso, Nancy Qian
items.summary: Foreign aid seeks to provide basic services, such as health care and education, to poor and vulnerable populations. Its effectiveness depends on last-mile delivery: whether those services reach the people who need them. This article reviews evidence on two key aspects of last-mile delivery.

items.headline: Irregular Demand: The Anti-Compromise Effect in the Field -- by Nicola Gennaioli, John A. List, Matthias Rodemeier, Gregory K. Sun
items.summary: Neoclassical demand obeys regularity: adding a good can only draw demand away from existing goods. In a natural field experiment with Lyft covering 7.2 million riders and 47 million choices, we randomize the presence and price of a premium ride. Contrary to regularity, the premium ride raises demand for the cheapest incumbent and for not buying.

items.headline: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
items.summary: Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient.

items.headline: Sharp Complexity Thresholds for Network Cournot Competition
items.summary: We determine the approximation complexity of network Cournot equilibrium as a function of demand degree and the number of firms sharing a market. For common, nonincreasing concave polynomial inverse demands, convex quadratic costs of firms' allocation vectors, and rational total capacities, high-precision approximation is polynomial-time solvable for cubic demands, regardless of market size. Quartic demands remain tractable when each market has at most three firms, and quintic demands remain tractable with at most two.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: These thresholds are exact: approximation at a fixed positive profit-regret tolerance is PPAD-hard for quartic demands with four firms per market, quintic demands with three, and sextic demands with two. Each hardness result uses one fixed demand curve in every market, a constant number of markets per firm, and globally nondecreasing strongly convex quadratic costs. We also give a polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary-degree nonincreasing concave polynomial demands when each firm's convex polynomial cost depends only on its total production. The algorithm assigns one marginal charge to each firm and adjusts the charges until each firm's total sales approximate the quantity it would produce at that charge.

items.headline: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2
items.summary: We construct a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order in which every online rule earns strictly less than $1/2$ of the expected offline optimum. A common partition, revealed at the third arrival, gives the first three buyers one unit of welfare per item. If the rule uses three distinct partitions, either an item allocated early contributes zero or the fourth buyer's expected value for the remaining bundle is one less than its size.

items.headline: Polycentrality in Urban Socioecological Systems: A Multilayer Analysis of Social Infrastructure in Iztapalapa, Mexico City
items.summary: The spatial distribution of infrastructure and activities, along with the networks and interactions that connect them, is key to understanding the relationship between urban form, function, and sustainability from a complex systems perspective. Within this dynamic relationship, the extent to which localized social infrastructure can reinforce existing functional centralities or create conditions for the emergence of new ones remains insufficiently understood. This study examines these relationships through the UTOPÍAS program in Iztapalapa, Mexico City, where 15 public social facilities have been established across a historically underserved urban territory.

items.headline: Modelling population distribution across cities on spatial networks using the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems
items.summary: We investigate the urban population distribution of the Italian region of Sardinia through the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems on spatial networks, interpreting cities both as agents and vertices of a graph, and representing interurban links as edges. We consider various emigration rules to model the interactions between agents, obtaining two main results: the bimodal lognormal fit of the total population distribution among cities and the Pareto fit of the tail. Overall, our model provides results consistent with the actual distribution derived from ISTAT data of Sardinia; furthermore, the bimodal lognormal fit generally follows the distribution tail more accurately than the Pareto one, although the two coincide in the first half.

items.headline: Amplifying or Redistributing Coupling: Synchronization in Sparse Adaptive Oscillator Networks
items.summary: Synchronization -- different units falling into a common rhythm -- matters in systems ranging from electrical generators to populations of neurons. But what happens when the connections that coordinate their timing can also change? If two units become more closely aligned and their connection strengthens, that extra influence can either increase the total coupling received by a unit or take a larger share of a fixed total.

detail.findings_tradeoffs: We examine these alternatives in a mathematical network of oscillators, each representing a repeating cycle, connected by sparse directed links. We compare constant connections with two adaptive rules that favor phase-aligned neighbors: unconstrained Hebbian coupling and homeostatic normalization, which keeps the total incoming effective coupling of each oscillator constant. Exact relationships establish this conservation and show that the mean Hebbian weight relaxes toward a value set by alignment along the network links. Longer observations reveal distinct individual trajectories, including increasing, sustained, and declining coherence. The central lesson is that the collective consequences of adaptation depend not only on which links are strengthened, but also on whether their strengthening adds influence or redistributes it.

items.headline: Neither graphs nor hypergraphs: structural moments of higher-order interactions determine stochastic social-impact dynamics
items.summary: Whether higher-order interactions can be reduced to simpler representations is a question about the dynamics they drive, not only about their structure: what can be discarded is whatever the dynamics does not see. We make this precise for binary-state stochastic dynamics in which each agent, when updated, interacts with a randomly selected group and changes state according to the fraction of disagreeing members, as in generalized voter and social-impact models on hypergraphs. We ask which statistics of the group-interaction process determine the resulting Markov dynamics.

items.headline: On the Complexity of Envy Cycle Elimination
items.summary: The envy cycle elimination (ECE) algorithm is a fundamental algorithm for the fair allocation of indivisible goods, guaranteeing an allocation that is envy-free up to one good under arbitrary monotone utilities. We show that the ECE algorithm can be implemented in $O(nm)$ time for $n$ agents and $m$ goods, and establish the tightness of this bound.

items.headline: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees for Goods and Chores
items.summary: We study temporal fair division of indivisible items in both the goods and chores settings, with $n \ge 2$ agents and nonnegative additive values or costs. Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival.

detail.method_architecture: Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival.
detail.findings_tradeoffs: For goods, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item (TPROP1), a $1/n$ approximation to temporal maximin share (TMMS), and a $1/(n-1)$ approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item (TEF1). The TMMS factor is optimal. For chores, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact TPROP1 and a $2-1/n$ approximation to TMMS. Classical scheduling lower bounds based on fixed sequences carry over to chores TMMS, establishing the optimality of this factor for $n=2,3$. For every $n \ge 2$, we further show that $2-1/n$ is the optimal TMMS factor subject to exact TPROP1. For every fixed $n \ge 3$ and every finite $β\ge 1$, we construct an instance of chores admitting no $β$-TEF1 allocation.

items.headline: Is China Misreading the Moment?
items.summary: When U.S. President Donald Trump lands in Shenzhen later this week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, he will sit down with Chinese leader Xi Jinping for the fourth time amid an unexpected détente between Washington and Beijing. The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have announced a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.

The trade war of 2025 is in abeyance, the two governments have announced a relationship of “constructive strategic stability,” and, to the alarm of American allies, Trump and Xi are planning to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Beneath the surface, however, the détente is beginning to crack.
